children: experimental drug sone-ve helped patients with advanced stomach cancer who had received at least two prior treatments to live longer than analysts had expected, according to late-stage trial data presented on Sunday.

Patients on the conjugate drug that links an antibody to a chemotherapy payload lived a median of 10 months, compared with 5 months on their doctor's choice of chemotherapy, a 53% reduction in the risk of death.
Analysts were expecting an overall survival hazard ratio, or risk of death, of about 0.7 or lower, with a gain of at least 2 months.

"A 5-month improvement in overall survival is very clinically significant in a difficult to treat patient population," said Susan Galbraith, executive vice president of oncology haematology research and development at AstraZeneca.
ASTRAZENECA INVESTS IN AND WORKS WITH SUMMIT THERAPEUTICS

The detailed data from the 532-patient study was presented at the conference of the European Society for Medical Oncology in Madrid on Sunday, a month after AstraZeneca agreed to invest $2 billion in the biopharmaceutical company Summit Therapeutics and to test sone-ve alongside Summit's bispecific antibody ivonescimab.

Patients with gastroesophageal cancer in AstraZeneca's study were enrolled if at least 25% of their tumour cells showed claudin 18.2, a protein found on many cancer cells. The approved treatment for this target requires a 75% cutoff.
Galbraith said the lower threshold could double the number of patients who would be able to receive treatment.

"I think that bodes well for the opportunity to move it into the earlier line setting," she told Reuters in an interview. Another study of more than 2,000 patients, is already testing the drug earlier in a patient's course of therapy.

Although overall survival was extended, progression-free survival, a co-main goal, did not reach statistical significance, with medians of 4.2 months on the drug and 3.8 on chemotherapy. Galbraith said progression is harder to measure in stomach cancer because tumours often spread in a diffuse way.
HSBC analysts said the miss makes it harder to compare the drug with IBI343, a rival claudin 18.2 therapy being developed by Takeda
, which succeeded on its progression-free survival goal in a late-stage study.
Serious side effects were less common with AstraZeneca's drug, 36.4% versus 44.8% on chemotherapy, though stomach-related side effects were more frequent, at 11.1% versus 6.3%.
